{{Short description|American cryptographer and classicist}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=January 2022}}
'''Charles Jastrow Mendelsohn''' (December 8, 1880 – September 27, 1939) was an [[Americans|American]] [[Cryptography|cryptographer]] and [[Classics|classicist]].<ref name=dict-north-carolina-biography>{{cite book|url=https://www.ncpedia.org/biography/mendelsohn-charles|title=Dictionary of North Carolina Biography|publisher=[[University of North Carolina Press]]|editor-link=[[William S. Powell]]|access-date=March 16, 2018}}</ref> He was the only child of [[Rabbi]] [[Samuel Mendelsohn]] and Esther Jastrow.<ref name=dict-north-carolina-biography/><ref name=jewish-encyclopedia-samuel-mendelsohn>{{cite book|url=http://www.jewishencyclopedia.com/articles/10662-mendelsohn-samuel|title=Jewish Encyclopedia|publisher=[[Funk & Wagnalls]]}}</ref><ref name=nc-dept-natural-cultural-wilmingtonian-decodes-german-war-correspondence>{{cite web|url=https://www.ncdcr.gov/blog/2017/11/09/wilmingtonian-decodes-german-war-correspondence|title=Wilmingtonian Decodes German War Correspondence|last=Bandel|first=Jessica|publisher=[[North Carolina Department of Natural and Cultural Resources]]|date=November 9, 2017|accessdate=March 16, 2018}}</ref>

He was born in [[Wilmington, North Carolina]].<ref name=dict-north-carolina-biography/>

==Education==
He graduated from the [[Episcopal Academy]], [[Philadelphia]] in 1896.<ref name=dict-north-carolina-biography/> He was a Harrison Scholar at the [[University of Pennsylvania]], which he graduated with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] in 1900 and a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in 1904.<ref name=dict-north-carolina-biography/> He was a member of [[Phi Beta Kappa]].<ref name=dict-north-carolina-biography/> He joined the faculty of [[City College of New York|College of the City of New York]] as a tutor in Greek in 1905, becoming an instructor in 1907.<ref name=dict-north-carolina-biography/> He was a professor of ancient languages in 1917.<ref name=nc-dept-natural-cultural-wilmingtonian-decodes-german-war-correspondence/>

==Military service==
During [[World War I]] he served in the censorship department of the [[United States Post Office Department|Post Office Department]] in 1917, dealing with foreign language, postal and newspaper censorship.<ref name=dict-north-carolina-biography/><ref name=nc-dept-natural-cultural-wilmingtonian-decodes-german-war-correspondence/> His work came to the attention of [[Herbert Yardley]] and he was recruited into  Military Intelligence, section 8 (MI-8).<ref name=nc-dept-natural-cultural-wilmingtonian-decodes-german-war-correspondence/> From 1918 to 1919 he was a captain in the Military Intelligence Division of the [[United States Department of War|War Department]] General Staff.<ref name=dict-north-carolina-biography/>

He led a team dealing with German diplomatic correspondence, breaking at least six diplomatic ciphers.<ref name=nc-dept-natural-cultural-wilmingtonian-decodes-german-war-correspondence/> Two messages dealt with German attempts to get support from Mexico.<ref name=nc-dept-natural-cultural-wilmingtonian-decodes-german-war-correspondence/>

He received an [[honorable discharge]].<ref name=nc-dept-natural-cultural-wilmingtonian-decodes-german-war-correspondence/>

==Return to civilian life==
He returned to City College in 1920 as a professor of history.<ref name=dict-north-carolina-biography/><ref name=nc-dept-natural-cultural-wilmingtonian-decodes-german-war-correspondence/> He remained interested in cryptography, writing papers and became interested in the history of the topic, collecting many books on it.<ref name=dict-north-carolina-biography/>

He remained in contact with Herbert Yardley and did part time cryptographic work for the [[Black Chamber]].<ref name=nc-dept-natural-cultural-wilmingtonian-decodes-german-war-correspondence/> Together they published the ''Universal Trade Code'', a commercial code.<ref name=nc-dept-natural-cultural-wilmingtonian-decodes-german-war-correspondence/> He wrote several works for the Black Chamber, including ''The Zimmermann Telegram of January 16, 1917, and its Cryptographic Background'' and ''Studies in German Diplomatic Codes Employed During the World War''.<ref name=nc-dept-natural-cultural-wilmingtonian-decodes-german-war-correspondence/>

==Death==
In 1939, he was recalled to active duty as a result of [[World War II]], but while preparing he contracted [[meningitis]] and died of it.<ref name=dict-north-carolina-biography/><ref name=nc-dept-natural-cultural-wilmingtonian-decodes-german-war-correspondence/>

His library, which had been called "probably the most important cryptographic library in America, if not in the world" was bequeathed to the University of Pennsylvania.<ref name=dict-north-carolina-biography/>

He had never married and was survived by his mother.<ref name=dict-north-carolina-biography/> He was buried in the Hebrew Cemetery at [[Oakdale Cemetery (Wilmington, North Carolina)|Oakdale Cemetery]], Wilmington, North Carolina.<ref name=dict-north-carolina-biography/>

==Publications==
*''Studies in the Word-Play in Plautus''<ref name=dict-north-carolina-biography/>
*''The Zimmermann Telegram of January 16, 1917, and its Cryptographic Background''<ref name=nc-dept-natural-cultural-wilmingtonian-decodes-german-war-correspondence/>
*''Studies in German Diplomatic Codes Employed During the World War''<ref name=nc-dept-natural-cultural-wilmingtonian-decodes-german-war-correspondence/>
